essential_elements: Clause (1): the State cannot confer non-military, non-academic titles — this is what underlies the National Awards (Bharat Ratna, Padma awards) being formally styled as non-titular civilian 'awards' or 'distinctions', not titles, following constitutional and judicial clarification (Balaji Raghavan case)
Clauses (2)-(4) form an escalating scheme regulating foreign honours/benefits based on citizenship and whether the recipient holds a State office of profit or trust
exceptions_and_qualifications: Military and academic distinctions are expressly excluded from clause (1)'s bar and may be freely conferred by the State
Presidential consent under clauses (3) and (4) is a case-specific safeguard, not a blanket permission — each acceptance requires its own consent
breakdown.how_to_read: Cite Article 18 whenever a dispute involves the constitutionality of State-conferred honours (distinguishing genuine 'titles' from permitted awards/distinctions) or a foreign-honours-acceptance controversy involving a public office-holder — the operative question is always whether presidential consent under clauses (3)/(4) was sought where required.

sections.title: Protection of certain rights regarding freedom of speech, etc.
sections.raw_text: (1) All citizens shall have the right— (a) to freedom of speech and expression; (b) to assemble peaceably and without arms; (c) to form associations or unions or co-operative societies; (d) to move freely throughout the territory of India; (e) to reside and settle in any part of the territory of India; and (g) to practise any profession, or to carry on any occupation, trade or business. (2) Nothing in sub-clause (a) of clause (1) shall affect the operation of any existing law, or prevent the State from making any law, in so far as such law imposes reasonable restrictions on the exercise of the right conferred by the said sub-clause in the interests of the sovereignty and integrity of India, the security of the State, friendly relations with foreign States, public order, decency or morality, or in relation to contempt of court, defamation or incitement to an offence. (3) Nothing in sub-clause (b) of the said clause shall affect the operation of any existing law in so far as it imposes, or prevent the State from making any law imposing, in the interests of the sovereignty and integrity of India or public order, reasonable restrictions on the exercise of the right conferred by the said sub-clause. (4) Nothing in sub-clause (c) of the said clause shall affect the operation of any existing law in so far as it imposes, or prevent the State from making any law imposing, in the interests of the sovereignty and integrity of India or public order or morality, reasonable restrictions on the exercise of the right conferred by the said sub-clause. (5) Nothing in sub-clauses (d) and (e) of the said clause shall affect the operation of any existing law in so far as it imposes, or prevent the State from making any law imposing, reasonable restrictions on the exercise of any of the rights conferred by the said sub-clauses either in the interests of the general public or for the protection of the interests of any Scheduled Tribe. (6) Nothing in sub-clause (g) of the said clause shall affect the operation of any existing law in so far as it imposes, or prevent the State from making any law imposing, in the interests of the general public, reasonable restrictions on the exercise of the right conferred by the said sub-clause, and, in particular, nothing in the said sub-clause shall affect the operation of any existing law in so far as it relates to, or prevent the State from making any law relating to,— (i) the professional or technical qualifications necessary for practising any profession or carrying on any occupation, trade or business, or (ii) the carrying on by the State, or by a corporation owned or controlled by the State, of any trade, business, industry or service, whether to the exclusion, complete or partial, of citizens or otherwise.
key_terms: State monopoly in trade or business

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 19(1) is the Constitution's core bundle of individual liberties for citizens: speech and expression, peaceable unarmed assembly, forming associations/unions/co-operative societies, free movement throughout India, residing and settling anywhere in India, and practising any profession or carrying on any occupation, trade, or business (the original property-right sub-clause (f) was removed in 1978, when the right to property was demoted from a fundamental right to Article 300A). None of these six freedoms is absolute — clauses (2) through (6) are mirror-image 'restriction clauses', one for each surviving sub-clause, letting the State impose 'reasonable restrictions' on specified public-interest grounds. Crucially, the grounds differ freedom by freedom (speech's grounds under clause 2 are the most numerous and specific, including sovereignty/integrity, State security, foreign relations, public order, decency/morality, contempt of court, defamation, and incitement to an offence), so each sub-clause must be checked against its own tailored restriction clause.
essential_elements: Clause (1) lists six substantive freedoms: speech/expression (a), peaceable assembly (b), association/union/co-operative society (c), movement (d), residence (e), and profession/occupation/trade/business (g)
Each restriction clause (2)-(6) is specific to one sub-clause and lists its own distinct permissible grounds for restriction
Restrictions must be 'reasonable' — an independent, judicially reviewable standard, not merely any restriction the State chooses to impose
Clause (6) additionally permits State monopolies (wholly or partly excluding citizens) in trade, business, industry, or service
exceptions_and_qualifications: Sub-clause (f) (the original right to acquire, hold, and dispose of property) was omitted by the Forty-fourth Amendment Act, 1978, and is no longer a Part III fundamental right — property is now protected only as a constitutional (not fundamental) right under Article 300A

The 'reasonableness' of a restriction is tested by courts considering the nature of the right, the extent and urgency of the evil sought to be remedied, proportionality of the restriction, and the manner of its imposition — not left to unreviewable legislative discretion
These six freedoms are available only to citizens, unlike Articles 14, 20, 21, and 22 which extend more broadly to 'persons'
breakdown.how_to_read: When analysing an Article 19 challenge, always identify (i) which specific sub-clause of clause (1) is invoked, (ii) whether the challenged restriction falls within that sub-clause's own tailored restriction clause (2)-(6), and (iii) whether the restriction is 'reasonable' on the facts — a restriction valid for one sub-clause's grounds cannot be borrowed to justify restricting a different freedom.

sections.title: Protection in respect of conviction for offences
sections.raw_text: (1) No person shall be convicted of any offence except for violation of a law in force at the time of the commission of the Act charged as an offence, nor be subjected to a penalty greater than that which might have been inflicted under the law in force at the time of the commission of the offence. (2) No person shall be prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once. (3) No person accused of any offence shall be compelled to be a witness against himself.
key_terms: protection against ex post facto law

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 20 provides three distinct criminal-law protections available to 'any person' (citizen or not), all non-suspendable even during a proclamation of Emergency. Clause (1) bars ex post facto criminal laws — a person cannot be convicted for an act that was not an offence when committed, nor punished more severely than the law in force at that time allowed. Clause (2) is the double jeopardy protection — no repeated prosecution and punishment for the same offence once already prosecuted and punished for it. Clause (3) is the privilege against self-incrimination — an accused person cannot be compelled to testify against themselves.
essential_elements: Clause (1): applies only to the imposition of criminal liability/penalty for an act not an offence at the time, or a penalty exceeding what the law then prescribed — it does not bar retrospective civil laws or procedural changes
Clause (2): 'prosecuted and punished' requires both a prior prosecution AND punishment for the very same offence — a mere prior prosecution that did not result in punishment does not trigger this bar

Clause (3): the compulsion must be to be a witness 'against himself' — it protects against compelled self-incriminatory testimonial communication, not all forms of evidence gathering (e.g., producing certain physical evidence, subject to scrutiny)
exceptions_and_qualifications: Clause (1) does not prevent a change in criminal procedure being applied retrospectively — only substantive offence-creation and penalty-enhancement are barred retrospectively

Clause (2)'s double jeopardy protection is narrower than some other jurisdictions' — it requires actual prior punishment, not merely a prior trial or acquittal (contrast with the statutory protection in the Cr.P.C./BNSS against second trial after acquittal or conviction)
Article 20's three protections are among the very few fundamental rights that Article 359 does not permit to be suspended during a National Emergency
breakdown.how_to_read: Article 20 is the standard citation for challenging retrospective criminal legislation (clause 1), a second prosecution for an identical offence already punished (clause 2), or coerced confessions/testimony (clause 3) — always confirm these protections remain available even during an Emergency, unlike most other Part III rights.

sections.title: Protection of life and personal liberty
sections.raw_text: No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law.

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 21, in just one sentence, has become the single most expansively interpreted provision of the Indian Constitution. On its face, it only guarantees that the State cannot deprive any person of life or personal liberty except through a 'procedure established by law' — originally read (in A.K. Gopalan) as merely requiring that some valid enacted procedure exist, however harsh. This changed fundamentally after Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978), which held that the 'procedure' itself must be fair, just, and reasonable (effectively importing a due-process-like standard) and that Articles 14, 19, and 21 are interlinked, not mutually exclusive silos. Since then, courts have read into 'life' and 'personal liberty' a vast range of unenumerated rights — including privacy, dignity, livelihood, health, a clean environment, speedy trial, legal aid, and shelter, among many others.
essential_elements: Applies to 'any person' (not just citizens), and protects both 'life' and 'personal liberty'
Deprivation must follow a 'procedure established by law' — post-Maneka Gandhi, that procedure must itself be fair, just, and reasonable, not merely enacted
The right has been judicially expanded to encompass numerous unenumerated rights considered essential to a life of dignity
exceptions_and_qualifications: Pre-Maneka Gandhi jurisprudence (A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras) treated 'procedure established by law' as a narrower guarantee than American 'due process of law', focused on mere existence of enacted procedure rather than its substantive fairness — this narrow view no longer represents the law
The right to privacy was expressly recognised as intrinsic to Article 21 (and Part III generally) in K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017), a landmark 9-judge bench decision
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat Article 21 as the Constitution's residuary reservoir of substantive liberty — when no other specific fundamental right precisely fits a claim involving bodily autonomy, dignity, livelihood, or procedural fairness in deprivation of liberty, Article 21 (read with the post-Maneka Gandhi fairness standard) is very likely the applicable provision, and always check whether the 'procedure' under challenge would itself survive a fairness/reasonableness test, not merely whether a procedure exists on paper.

sections.title: Right to education
sections.raw_text: The State shall provide free and compulsory education to all children of the age of six to fourteen years in such manner as the State may, by law, determine.

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 21A, inserted in 2002, elevates elementary education from a mere Directive Principle (it was previously only aspirational under Article 45) to an enforceable fundamental right. It obliges the State to provide free and compulsory education to every child aged six to fourteen, with the precise implementation manner left to be determined by law — which Parliament did through the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 (the RTE Act).
essential_elements: The right is age-bound: specifically children between six and fourteen years
The obligation is on 'the State' to provide education that is both free and compulsory
The 'manner' of providing this education is left to be determined by law — i.e., this Article is not fully self-executing without implementing legislation
exceptions_and_qualifications: Education for children below six or above fourteen (e.g., early childhood care, or secondary/higher education) is not directly guaranteed as a fundamental right under this Article, though early childhood care up to age six is separately addressed as a Directive Principle under the amended Article 45

The RTE Act, 2009 is the primary implementing legislation giving Article 21A operational content — including provisions on neighbourhood schools, 25% reservation for disadvantaged groups in private unaided schools, and prohibition of detention/expulsion up to a certain class
breakdown.how_to_read: Article 21A must always be read together with the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 for its practical content — the Article establishes the fundamental right in principle, but the Act supplies the operative rules (admission age, curriculum standards, private-school obligations, etc.).

sections.title: Protection against arrest and detention in certain cases
sections.raw_text: (1) No person who is arrested shall be detained in custody without being informed, as soon as may be, of the grounds for such arrest nor shall he be denied the right to consult, and to be defended by, a legal practitioner of his choice. (2) Every person who is arrested and detained in custody shall be produced before the nearest magistrate within a period of twenty-four hours of such arrest excluding the time necessary for the journey from the place of arrest to the court of the magistrate and no such person shall be detained in custody beyond the said period without the authority of a magistrate. (3) Nothing in clauses (1) and (2) shall apply— (a) to any person who for the time being is an enemy alien; or (b) to any person who is arrested or detained under any law providing for preventive detention. (4) No law providing for preventive detention shall authorise the detention of a person for a longer period than three months unless— (a) an Advisory Board consisting of persons who are, or have been, or are qualified to be appointed as, Judges of a High Court has reported before the expiration of the said period of three months that there is in its opinion sufficient cause for such detention: Provided that nothing in this sub-clause shall authorise the detention of any person beyond the maximum period prescribed by any law made by Parliament under sub-clause (b) of clause (7); or (b) such person is detained in accordance with the provisions of any law made by Parliament under sub-clauses (a) and (b) of clause (7). (5) When any person is detained in pursuance of an order made under any law providing for preventive detention, the authority making the order shall, as soon as may be, communicate to such person the grounds on which the order has been made and shall afford him the earliest opportunity of making a representation against the order. (6) Nothing in clause (5) shall require the authority making any such order as is referred to in that clause to disclose facts which such authority considers to be against the public interest to disclose. (7) Parliament may by law prescribe— (a) the circumstances under which, and the class or classes of cases in which, a person may be detained for a period longer than three months under any law providing for preventive detention without obtaining the opinion of an Advisory Board in accordance with the provisions of sub-clause (a) of clause (4); (b) the maximum period for which any person may in any class or classes of cases be detained under any law providing for preventive detention; and (c) the procedure to be followed by an Advisory Board in an inquiry under sub-clause (a) of clause (4).

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 22 splits arrest/detention protections into two very different tracks. Clauses (1)-(2) protect ordinary (punitive) arrestees: the right to be told the grounds of arrest promptly, the right to consult and be defended by a lawyer of choice, and the right to be produced before a magistrate within 24 hours (excluding travel time), with no custody beyond that period without magisterial authorisation. Clause (3) carves out two categories from these protections entirely — enemy aliens, and anyone arrested/detained under a preventive detention law. Clauses (4)-(7) then set up a separate, more limited protective scheme specifically for preventive detention (confinement to prevent anticipated future harm, not to punish a past offence): ordinarily capping detention beyond three months unless an Advisory Board of High-Court-qualified persons certifies sufficient cause, requiring communication of detention grounds and an opportunity to make a representation (subject to a public-interest non-disclosure carve-out), and leaving Parliament to legislate the finer procedural details.
essential_elements: Clauses (1)-(2) are the baseline protections for ordinary arrest: grounds disclosure, right to counsel, and 24-hour magistrate production
Clause (3) removes these baseline protections entirely for enemy aliens and for persons held under preventive detention laws

Clauses (4)-(7) substitute a different, narrower set of safeguards specifically for preventive detention: the three-month Advisory Board check, grounds communication, representation opportunity (clause 5), and a public-interest non-disclosure exception (clause 6)
exceptions_and_qualifications: Preventive detention is a striking constitutional anomaly — confinement without trial, justified by anticipated rather than committed wrongdoing — and Article 22's own safeguards for it are considerably weaker than the ordinary-arrest protections in clauses (1)-(2)

A Forty-fourth Amendment Act, 1978 substitution of clause (4) (shortening the default period to two months and reworking the Advisory Board composition) was enacted but has never been brought into force by notification, so the original three-month scheme printed here remains the operative law
The public-interest non-disclosure carve-out in clause (6) has been strictly construed by courts to prevent it from swallowing the representation right in clause (5)
breakdown.how_to_read: Always separate an Article 22 analysis into the two tracks — first ask whether the detention is ordinary/punitive (clauses 1-2 apply in full) or preventive (clauses 3-7 apply instead, with the specific procedural safeguards of clauses 4-7 substituting for clauses 1-2) — and note that the harsher, unnotified 1978 amendment to clause (4) is not yet in force, so the original three-month/Advisory-Board text governs in practice.

sections.title: Prohibition of traffic in human beings and forced labour
sections.raw_text: (1) Traffic in human beings and begar and other similar forms of forced labour are prohibited and any contravention of this provision shall be an offence punishable in accordance with law. (2) Nothing in this article shall prevent the State from imposing compulsory service for public purposes, and in imposing such service the State shall not make any discrimination on grounds only of religion, race, caste or class or any of them.

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 23, like Article 17, operates horizontally — directly against private individuals, not merely the State. It prohibits human trafficking and 'begar' (a traditional term for labour exacted without payment) and other forms of forced labour, making any contravention a punishable offence. Clause (2) carves out compulsory public service (such as conscription-type civic duties) as permissible, but even here the State cannot discriminate in imposing that service on grounds only of religion, race, caste, or class.
essential_elements: Prohibition covers human trafficking and begar/forced labour in any similar form, enforceable against private persons as well as the State
Contravention is made a punishable offence, with the specific offence and penalty left to ordinary law
Clause (2) permits State-imposed compulsory service for public purposes, subject to a non-discrimination proviso on the listed grounds
exceptions_and_qualifications: The Supreme Court in People's Union for Democratic Rights v. Union of India (1982) held that paying wages below the statutory minimum wage amounts to 'forced labour' under Article 23, significantly widening the provision's reach beyond literal bonded labour
The Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976 is the principal legislation giving Article 23 further statutory content
breakdown.how_to_read: Article 23 is a rare horizontally-enforceable right — use it directly against private employers or individuals engaged in trafficking, bonded labour, or forced/underpaid labour, and remember the expanded 'forced labour' definition covering sub-minimum-wage work established in the PUDR case.

sections.title: Prohibition of employment of children in factories, etc.
sections.raw_text: No child below the age of fourteen years shall be employed to work in any factory or mine or engaged in any other hazardous employment.

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 24 bars the employment of children below fourteen years in factories, mines, or any other hazardous work, protecting children from exploitative and dangerous labour during their formative years. Like Articles 17 and 23, it is understood to operate against both State and private employers.
essential_elements: The prohibition applies specifically to children below fourteen years of age
It covers employment in factories, mines, and 'any other hazardous employment' — a category courts and legislation have further defined
It operates against private employers as well as the State
exceptions_and_qualifications: The Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986 (renamed and amended as the Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act) is the principal statute implementing this Article, specifying the list of hazardous occupations and processes and providing enforcement mechanisms

Non-hazardous family-enterprise or artistic work by children, subject to statutory conditions, has historically been treated differently under the implementing legislation, though this remains a contested policy area
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 24 together with Article 21A (right to education) and Article 39(e)-(f) (Directive Principles on child welfare) as a cluster of child-protection provisions, and consult the Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act for the operative list of hazardous occupations/processes.

sections.title: Freedom of conscience and free profession, practice and propagation of religion
sections.raw_text: (1) Subject to public order, morality and health and to the other provisions of this Part, all persons are equally entitled to freedom of conscience and the right freely to profess, practice and propagate religion. (2) Nothing in this article shall affect the operation of any existing law or prevent the State from making any law— (a) regulating or restricting any economic, financial, political or other secular activity which may be associated with religious practice; (b) providing for social welfare and reform or the throwing open of Hindu religious institutions of a public character to all classes and sections of Hindus. Explanation I.—The wearing and carrying of kirpans shall be deemed to be included in the profession of the Sikh religion. Explanation II.—In sub-clause (b) of clause (2), the reference to Hindus shall be construed as including a reference to persons professing the Sikh, Jaina or Buddhist religion, and the reference to Hindu religious institutions shall be construed accordingly.
key_terms: secular activity associated with religious practice
throwing open of Hindu religious institutions

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 25 guarantees every person — not just citizens — freedom of conscience and the right to freely profess, practice, and propagate their religion, though this is expressly made 'subject to public order, morality and health' and to the other Part III rights. Clause (2) preserves the State's power to regulate secular activities merely associated with religious practice (e.g., economic or political aspects of a religious institution's operation) and to enact social-welfare/reform laws, including opening Hindu religious institutions of a public character to all classes and sections of Hindus. Explanation I specifically protects a Sikh's wearing and carrying of a kirpan as part of religious profession. Explanation II clarifies that wherever clause (2)(b) refers to 'Hindus' and 'Hindu religious institutions', this is deemed to include Sikhs, Jains, and Buddhists and their institutions — reflecting the historical (and still debated) constitutional classification of these communities for this specific purpose.
essential_elements: The right belongs to 'all persons' and covers three distinct freedoms: freedom of conscience, and the rights to profess, practice, and propagate religion
The right is expressly subject to public order, morality, health, and the rest of Part III — it is not absolute
Clause (2)(a) preserves State power over secular activities merely associated with religion (e.g., managing temple finances)
Clause (2)(b) preserves State power for social welfare/reform and opening Hindu (and by Explanation II, Sikh/Jain/Buddhist) religious institutions to all classes
exceptions_and_qualifications: 'Propagate' has been judicially construed to mean transmitting or spreading one's own religious beliefs through exposition, not a right to forcibly convert another person (Rev. Stanislaus v. State of Madhya Pradesh)

Explanation II's inclusion of Sikhs, Jains, and Buddhists within 'Hindus' is limited strictly to clause (2)(b)'s social-welfare/temple-access purpose — it does not mean these communities are treated as Hindus for all other constitutional or legal purposes
breakdown.how_to_read: Article 25 is the starting point for any freedom-of-religion analysis — always separate the core religious/conscience claim (protected, subject to public order/morality/health) from any 'secular activity merely associated with' the religious practice (which the State can regulate under clause 2(a)) — this distinction (the 'essential religious practices' test) is the recurring battleground in Indian religious-freedom litigation.

sections.title: Freedom to manage religious affairs
sections.raw_text: Subject to public order, morality and health, every religious denomination or any section thereof shall have the right— (a) to establish and maintain institutions for religious and charitable purposes; (b) to manage its own affairs in matters of religion; (c) to own and acquire movable and immovable property; and (d) to administer such property in accordance with law.
key_terms: right to own and acquire property (religious institutions)

breakdown.plain_summary: While Article 25 protects the individual's freedom of religion, Article 26 protects the collective/institutional freedom of a 'religious denomination' (or a section of one) — again subject to public order, morality, and health. It guarantees four specific rights: establishing and maintaining religious and charitable institutions, managing the denomination's own religious affairs, owning and acquiring property, and administering that property, though the last right is qualified by 'in accordance with law' (meaning ordinary property/administration law can regulate how such property is managed, even though the right to manage religious affairs proper is more strongly insulated).
essential_elements: The right-holder is a 'religious denomination or any section thereof', not merely an individual — courts have developed a specific test for what qualifies as a 'religious denomination' (a common faith, common organisation, and a distinctive name)
Sub-clause (b) — managing 'matters of religion' — is the most strongly protected limb, closely tied to the 'essential religious practices' doctrine

Sub-clause (d) — administering property — is explicitly made subject to ordinary law, unlike sub-clause (b), giving the State greater regulatory latitude over property administration than over core religious affairs
exceptions_and_qualifications: The distinction between 'matters of religion' (protected, largely insulated from ordinary regulation) and 'secular'/administrative matters merely associated with religion (regulable by the State, especially given sub-clause (d)'s 'in accordance with law' qualifier) is the central interpretive battleground under this Article, mirroring the same essential-practices analysis under Article 25
breakdown.how_to_read: When a religious institution's internal governance is challenged, ask first whether the matter is a genuinely 'essential religious practice'/'matter of religion' under sub-clause (b) (strongly protected) or a property-administration matter under sub-clause (d) (subject to ordinary regulatory law) — the answer to this threshold question usually decides the case.

sections.title: Freedom as to payment of taxes for promotion of any particular religion
sections.raw_text: No person shall be compelled to pay any taxes, the proceeds of which are specifically appropriated in payment of expenses for the promotion or maintenance of any particular religion or religious denomination.
key_terms: tax for promotion of a particular religion

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 27 embodies religious neutrality in public finance: no one can be compelled to pay a tax whose proceeds are specifically earmarked to promote or maintain a particular religion or denomination. This targets 'tax' (a compulsory levy for general public purposes) specifically — a general grant-in-aid or a 'fee' charged for specific services rendered to a religious institution (e.g., regulatory or administrative fees) is treated differently and does not automatically fall foul of this Article.
essential_elements: The bar applies to 'taxes' whose proceeds are specifically appropriated for promoting or maintaining a particular religion or denomination

General taxation that merely happens to fund composite State expenditure (which might incidentally benefit religious institutions among many other things) does not violate this Article, since there is no specific appropriation for a particular religion
exceptions_and_qualifications: Courts distinguish a 'tax' (compulsory exaction for general public purposes, no direct quid pro quo) from a 'fee' (a charge for specific services rendered, e.g., regulating or supervising a temple's secular administration), and fees of the latter kind have generally been upheld as not attracting Article 27's bar
breakdown.how_to_read: Article 27 is narrowly targeted — before invoking it, confirm the levy in question is genuinely a 'tax' with proceeds specifically earmarked for a particular religion's promotion/maintenance, rather than a general tax or a regulatory fee for secular administrative services connected to a religious institution.

sections.title: Freedom as to attendance at religious instruction or religious worship in certain educational institutions
sections.raw_text: (1) No religious instruction shall be provided in any educational institution wholly maintained out of State funds. (2) Nothing in clause (1) shall apply to an educational institution which is administered by the State but has been established under any endowment or trust which requires that religious instruction shall be imparted in such institution. (3) No person attending any educational institution recognised by the State or receiving aid out of State funds shall be required to take part in any religious instruction that may be imparted in such institution or to attend any religious worship that may be conducted in such institution or in any premises attached thereto unless such person or, if such person is a minor, his guardian has given his consent thereto.
key_terms: consent for religious instruction or worship

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 28 addresses religion in education across a spectrum of institution types. Clause (1) flatly bars religious instruction in any institution wholly maintained out of State funds — full State funding means full religious neutrality. Clause (2) carves out an exception: if the State administers an institution that was established under a trust/endowment specifically requiring religious instruction (e.g., a formerly private religious college later taken over by the State but bound by its founding trust terms), that requirement can continue. Clause (3) covers a third category — institutions merely 'recognised' by the State or receiving State aid (but not wholly State-maintained) — where religious instruction/worship may occur, but no student (or, if a minor, their guardian) can be compelled to participate without consent.
essential_elements: Clause (1): wholly State-maintained institutions — religious instruction is completely barred
Clause (2): State-administered institutions bound by a founding trust/endowment requiring religious instruction — the exception preserves that requirement

Clause (3): State-recognised or State-aided (but not wholly State-run) institutions — religious instruction/worship may occur, but attendance/participation requires the student's (or minor's guardian's) consent
exceptions_and_qualifications: The three clauses create a graduated scheme based on the degree of State involvement (wholly funded vs. State-administered-but-trust-bound vs. merely recognised/aided) — the applicable rule depends entirely on correctly categorising the institution
Consent under clause (3) must be free and can be withheld even after initial enrolment, protecting ongoing rather than merely one-time choice
breakdown.how_to_read: When analysing a religious-instruction dispute in an educational institution, first classify the institution correctly among the three categories (wholly State-funded / State-administered-but-endowment-bound / merely recognised-or-aided) — the entire Article 28 analysis turns on this classification, and clause (3)'s consent requirement is the most commonly litigated limb in practice.
